newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia sets new interbank trading rules.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia sets new interbank trading rules.

text.p: Bank Negara Malaysia announced that finance companies wanting to trade in the interbank money market must raise their shareholders' funds to at least 350 million ringgit by January 1, 1998.
This would be further increased to 600 million ringgit by January 1, 1999, Bank Negara Governor Ahmad Mohd Don said at the Forex Association of Malaysia's annual dinner on Saturday.
"In general, size has become an increasingly important factor to gain competitiveness," the governor said in a speech released to the media on Monday.
"Among the interbank money market players, I note that a number of institutions are still under-capitalised. I would urge these institutions to build up their size and capacity," he said.
The governor also announced that to promote the bond market, the central bank would be introducing securities borrowing and lending to help increase liquidity in the market.
Securities borrowing and lending would allow banks to short sell bonds and thus help increase liquidity, analysts said.
The governor said the Fully Automated Tendering System, which was introduced for short and medium-term notes, will be extended to corporate bonds.
Ahmad said banking institutions would also have to create infrastructure to be able to sell bonds to individuals.
"With this development, market participants are expected to play a more significant role in the secondary market for bonds," the governor said.
He also announced that Bank of Commerce, Hongkong Bank Malaysia and Commerce International Merchant Bankers would be appointed principal dealers to Bank Negara.
They join 13 existing principal dealers, who are responsible for development of the local bond market through obligatory two-way quotes.
"At the same time, those that have not performed up to the mark will be given a period of six months to meet the current criteria," Ahmad warned existing principal dealers.
